title: Collateral types that fall below 20 million in debt must be offboarded, treating protocol complexity as a risk in itself
content:
A.3.7.1.1.3.1 states that "to protect the Protocol from unnecessary complexity, the Core Facilitator **must** offboard collateral types... if they fall below a total debt of 20 million."

The justification is not risk from the collateral asset itself but complexity — every live vault type carries fifteen or so parameters that must be monitored, re-justified, and kept current (A.3.7.1.1.2.5 requires the parameters be "regularly monitored and updated if needed"). A collateral type with little debt generates negligible revenue while consuming the same review attention as a large one, so the maintenance burden per unit of value becomes unfavourable.

Making it a *must* rather than a discretionary judgement is what gives the rule force. Left to case-by-case decisions, small vault types accumulate: each individually is cheap to keep and has some constituency, while the aggregate governance load grows unnoticed. A hard threshold removes the per-case debate.

A.3.7.1.1.3.3 handles everything else with the opposite posture — other collateral is offboarded "when the Core Facilitator deems it appropriate and when new mechanisms are in place to take over the roles previously covered." So the Atlas distinguishes low-usage collateral (offboard automatically) from functionally load-bearing collateral (offboard only once replaced), and A.3.7.1.1.3.4 routes both through the Operational Weekly Cycle.
description: A.3.7.1.1.3.1 makes offboarding mandatory rather than discretionary at that threshold, on the stated ground of protecting the Protocol from unnecessary complexity.
